items.title: FOMC Leaves Rate Unchanged
items.description: Economic Coverage FOMC Leaves Rate Unchanged By Danielle Hale Oct 28, 2026 The Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee (FOMC), the rate-setting body that meets roughly eight times per year, left the Federal Funds rate unchanged at its October meeting in a target range of 3.75 to 4.0 percent. This hold follows a 25 basis point hike in September, and was supported by 10 of the 12 voting members. Two voters, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, dissented, because they preferred to raise the rate by a quarter percentage point instead of holding. Even though the Fed left its policy rate unchanged in October, the market is anticipating another 2 to 3 hikes over the next 6 to 8 months which would mean a high-end rate range of 4.5 to 4.75 percent. This is slightly above the high-end of Fed funds rate projections made in September, and would position the Fed funds rate roughly halfway between its December 2025 to September 2026 low of 3.5 to 3.75 percent and its 5.25 to 5.5 percent prior peak. While the market and the Fed both seem to agree that some monetary policy restriction is warranted, most investors currently expect more restriction than the Fed has projected. Why further rate hikes are expected Since the September FOMC meeting, when the Fed pushed its rate 25 basis points higher, companies slowed hiring and summer job gains were revised down by 60,000 jobs . The unemployment rate remains relatively stable at 4.2 percent and layoffs are low, but the labor market is less dynamic than is ideal. Meanwhile, inflation surprised to the upside, with the CPI rising 0.6% in September, bringing the annual headline inflation rate to 3.7% as the cost of gas and energy rose sharply. Energy was not the only driver, however, and core CPI, which strips out the cost of food and energy, rose 2.6% in September. Taken together, these indicators suggest that the Fed is likely to continue its focus on inflation, which will likely warrant additional rate hikes. What this means for housing, and homebuyers and sellers Investors have made a round-trip in risk pricing since just before the September Fed meeting. The 10-year yield rose from just under 5 percent to more than 5.3 percent before dipping just under 5 percent in recent days, while mortgage rates climbed from just below 7 percent to more than 7.4 percent. Mortgage rates have not dropped back to their mid-September level, and the housing market is feeling the effects. Pending home sales in September dropped to their lowest level on record according to the National Association of Realtors as buyers and sellers have largely disengaged with the housing market for now. In August and September, existing-home sales dropped below a 4 million sales pace, and are likely to remain low through the rest of the year. Home shoppers shopping in this environment can still set themselves up for a better mortgage rate by boosting their credit, making a higher down payment, and, most importantly, shopping around for a mortgage. Those hoping to make a home purchase in the months ahead should plan for further mortgage rate volatility and rate-proof their home shopping budget by testing out a range of possible mortgage rates so they’ll be prepared to react.

items.title: Homeownership Rate Holds at 65.5% in Q3
items.description: Economic Coverage , Homeownership Homeownership Rate Holds at 65.5% in Q3 By Hannah Jones Oct 28, 2026 2026 Q3 Homeownership and Housing Vacancy Key Takeaways Homeownership rate holds steady. The U.S. homeownership rate was 65.5% in Q3 2026, statistically unchanged from both the prior quarter (65.0%) and a year earlier (65.3%). The rate continues to plateau in a narrow low-to-mid-65% band, with affordability pressures and limited supply showing little sign of easing their grip on the market. Homeowner vacancy remains low and steady. The homeowner vacancy rate held at 1.2% in Q3, virtually unchanged from both the prior quarter and a year earlier. Rental vacancy reaches its highest level in over a decade. The rental vacancy rate rose to 7.6%, up both quarter-over-quarter (7.3%) and year-over-year (7.1%), its highest level since 2014. Renting remains a critical pressure valve, though conditions vary by geography. With a national rental vacancy rate of 7.6%, rental markets continue to offer more flexibility for households unable to buy. Principal cities (8.8%) remain looser than suburbs (6.5%) and non-metro areas (6.4%), which were statistically similar to each other. The South leads in vacancy levels, while the Northeast and West saw the clearest year-over-year shifts. The South posted the highest rental vacancy rate (9.2%) and homeowner vacancy rate (1.5%) of any region, though neither was statistically different from a year ago. Rental vacancy rose significantly in the Northeast (5.0% to 6.2%) and the West (6.0% to 6.7%). Ownership slipped among 35-to-44-year-olds, while older households gained. Homeownership among 35-to-44-year-olds fell from 61.1% to 60.1% year-over-year. Households under 35 remain the lowest at 36.6%, statistically unchanged from 37.5% a year earlier. Meanwhile, 65+ homeownership rose from 77.9% to 79.1%. Racial ownership gaps remain entrenched. Homeownership among Black households fell from 45.7% to 44.4% year-over-year, while White homeownership rose from 74.0% to 75.1%. All other groups did not see statistically significant shifts. What happened this quarter The U.S. homeownership rate held at 65.5% in the third quarter of 2026, statistically unchanged compared with both the prior quarter (65.0%) and a year earlier (65.3%). While the rate remains within the narrow low-to-mid-65% range that has characterized the market in recent years, it continues to run well below the 2020 pandemic-era peak. Mortgage rates pushed back above 7% in late September for the first time in more than a year, which could weigh on would-be buyers heading into the fourth quarter. The homeowner vacancy rate held at 1.2% in Q3 2026, virtually the same as the previous quarter and the previous year. While homeowner vacancy remains below pre-pandemic norms, the recent pick up in inventory could mean vacancy drifts higher if demand is not sufficient to absorb supply. The rental vacancy rate rose to 7.6% in the third quarter, higher than both the previous quarter (7.3%) and the previous year (7.1%). With mortgage rates moving back above 7%, renting continues to stand out as a more affordable alternative to homeownership. However, climbing rental vacancy suggests that units are sitting empty as affordability pressure may discourage household formation. Vacancy was highest in principal cities (8.8%). Suburbs (6.5%) and non-metro areas (6.4%) were lower and not statistically different from each other. Regional differences remain pronounced . The South recorded the highest rental vacancy rate at 9.2%, followed by the Midwest (7.1%), the West (6.7%), and the Northeast (6.2%). The Midwest was higher than the Northeast and statistically similar to the West, while the Northeast and West were not statistically different from each other. Of the four regions, only the Northeast (up from 5.0%) and West (up from 6.0%) saw a statistically significant year-over-year increase in rental vacancy. Rental vacancy has stalled in the South as the wave of supply has subsided . The post-pandemic construction boom flooded these markets with new supply, but as multifamily construction has slowed, vacancy growth has stalled. On the ownership side, the South again led with the highest homeowner vacancy rate at 1.5%, while the other three regions saw vacancy between 0.9% and 1.1%. The Midwest continues to stand out for its high homeownership rate, reaching 69.5% in Q3 2026, though not statistically different from a year earlier, and remains well above the South (67.2%), Northeast (62.9%), and West (60.6%). Different outcomes by race/ethnicity Homeownership rates by race and ethnicity were mixed year over year. In the third quarter, the rate for non-Hispanic White householders rose to 75.1% from 74.0%, while the rate for Asian, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander householders was statistically unchanged at 62.3%. The rate for Black householders fell to 44.4% from 45.7%, and the rate for Hispanic householders was statistically unchanged at 48.1%. The gap between the highest and lowest rates remains more than 30 percentage points, underscoring the persistence of structural barriers to ownership. Different outcomes by age Ownership among younger households remains low, while older householders saw improvement. Homeownership among those under 35 was the lowest of any age group at 36.6%, statistically unchanged from 37.5% a year earlier. Homeownership among households aged 35 to 44 fell from 61.1% in Q3 of 2025 to 60.1% in Q3 of 2026. Ownership in the 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 cohorts held steady at 70.4% and 75.4%, respectively, while the 65+ group saw a 1.2 percentage point improvement to 79.1%. Ample starter-home inventory is crucial for young homeownership, and availability varies significantly across the country .

items.title: Down Payment Assistance Could Cut the Time to Save for a Home by a Year and a Half or More
items.description: Down Payment Assistance Could Cut the Time to Save for a Home by a Year and a Half or More Nationally, a 3.5% down payment boost allows a typical buyer to save for a 10% down payment 35% faster October 28, 2026 Anushna Prakash Written by Anushna Prakash Key findings: A median-income household could save 10% down on the typical U.S. home after 4.2 years, according to Zillow’s estimates. With down payment assistance covering 3.5% of that, the time to save would be cut to 2.7 years. Moving from a 6.5% down payment to 10% on a typical U.S. home would save a buyer $1,080 per year in monthly payments. Nationally, those monthly savings would bring an additional 26,338 homes within reach for a median-income buyer. Saving 10% down on the typical U.S. home takes the median household an estimated 4.2 years, or about four years and two months. With a down payment assistance program covering 3.5% of that 10% down payment, the same household could have enough saved a year and a half sooner. The same assistance also lowers a typical buyer’s mortgage payments by $1,080 a year, putting more homes within reach. Nationally, about 26,300 more active listings would become affordable in this scenario. For this analysis, Zillow is assuming a buyer puts a total of 10% down and receives an FHA loan . However, the minimum down payment for an FHA loan is 3.5%, meaning a buyer could also use this level of assistance to cover the entirety of their down payment. Making a smaller down payment does bring up the monthly mortgage payment some, but is a viable option for a buyer with the financial means to cover the monthly payment but without the necessary savings for a down payment. Zillow research has shown that one in five renter households headed by someone ages 29 to 43 could afford the monthly cost of owning a typical home in their market with just 5% down. A 3.5% boost cuts the time to save a 10% down payment by as much as 3.2 years Nationally, a median-income household saving for a 10% down payment on a typical U.S. home needs 4.2 years. That number could be cut to 2.7 years with a 3.5% boost from down payment assistance, a difference of 1.5 years. The benefit is biggest for a buyer in some of the most expensive metro areas, led by Los Angeles, where the years to save fall from 9.1 years to 5.9 years, putting homeownership within reach more than three years sooner. Three other major California metros see gaps of more than two and a half years: San Jose (8.5 years to 5.5 years with down payment assistance), San Diego (7.9 to 5.1) and San Francisco (7.7 to 5). Pittsburgh is the only major metro area where down payment assistance does not shave at least a year off the time needed to save 10% down on a typical home. A median-income Pittsburgh household could save 10% down after 2.7 years, which would be shortened to 1.8 years with down payment assistance. Lower payments save buyers $1,080 a year, bringing more listings within budget With a 6.5% down payment and a 6.78% mortgage rate (the average rate for an FHA loan in September), the monthly payment on a $366,157 home (the typical home value in September, according to the Zillow Home Value Index) would have been $3,010, including estimates for taxes, insurance and maintenance. If given a 3.5% boost via down payment assistance, that same home purchase would come with a monthly payment of $2,920, a savings of $1,080 per year. The annual savings are largest in San Jose ($4,608), San Francisco ($3,396), Los Angeles ($2,880), San Diego ($2,808) and New York ($2,160). Those monthly payment savings can bring more homes within reach. Nationally, 359,434 active listings were affordable to this hypothetical buyer with 6.5% down in September, representing 25.7% of what was listed for sale. With the 3.5% down payment assistance, 26,338 more listings would have been affordable, raising the share of affordable listings to 27.6%. Receiving 3.5% in down payment assistance would have brought the most listings newly within reach in Dallas (864), Atlanta (712), Miami (558) and Washington, D.C. (555). How the numbers work For years-to-save calculations , Zillow assumes a median-income household saves 10% of its income each month. This analysis assumes a household is buying the typical home in a given metro, as measured by the Zillow Home Value Index as of September 2026 . This analysis assumes a buyer is receiving an FHA loan, aligning with the down payment assistance program recently announced by Zillow Home Loans. Monthly housing costs assume a buyer purchases the typical home in a given metro, as measured by the Zillow Home Value Index as of September 2026. Estimates assume a mortgage rate of 6.78%, the average for an FHA loan in September, and include estimates for taxes, insurance and maintenance. Homes are considered affordable if the household would spend no more than 30% of its income on the total monthly payment. items.title: Fed Holds Rates, With Two Votes for Another Hike
items.description: Fed Holds Rates, With Two Votes for Another Hike October 28, 2026 Robert Dietz No Comments The Federal Reserve maintained the federal funds rate at a target range of 3.75% to 4% at the conclusion of its October policy meeting. Approved by a 10–2 vote, the decision followed September’s quarter-point increase. Federal Open Market Committee members Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented, supporting another 25-basis-point increase for October. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) upgraded its assessment of economic growth, describing activity as expanding at a “strong pace,” compared with a “solid pace” in September. This change suggests greater confidence in the economy’s momentum despite elevated uncertainty. The committee also cited resilient domestic spending. Geopolitical developments remain a source of uncertainty, although Chairman Warsh was positive about the economic outlook at his press conference. The Fed also emphasized that “Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust.” This productivity assessment is a possible favorable signal for the inflation outlook. Greater output per worker, via tech investment, can help contain labor costs, allowing the economy to grow without an increase in price pressures. Stronger growth alone therefore does not necessarily imply a need for tighter monetary policy, particularly if investment is expanding the economy’s productive capacity. On inflation, the committee maintained its assessment that price pressures remain elevated. The committee noted that it wanted to see an accumulation of more information before determining the appropriate policy stance to ensure a timely return of inflation to its two percent goal. This emphasis on additional data leaves the possibility of additional rate hikes in the future (NAHB is forecasting an increase in December), while also allowing the Fed to avoid raising rates immediately before the November election. September’s economic projections from the Fed pointed to an additional quarter-point increase before year-end. Today’s statement reiterated that “The Committee will deliver price stability.” The two dissents demonstrate that some FOMC voting members already see sufficient justification for another increase. For the majority, however, holding rates steady provides more time to evaluate inflation and the effects of September’s action. Separately, one could argue that tighter monetary policy from the Fed at this moment can do little to address a major source of recent inflation pressure: the Iran war. The policy challenge remains distinguishing temporary price increases from persistent inflation. September’s consumer price index (CPI) rose 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August, while core CPI, excluding food and energy, increased 2.6%, up from 2.4%. Gasoline accounted for more than half of the monthly headline increase, underscoring the importance of energy costs and geopolitical factors, although the rise in core inflation indicates that price pressures extend beyond energy. For housing, today’s hold on monetary policy avoids another increase in the policy rate that influences builder acquisition, development, and construction lending costs. However, financing conditions remain restrictive for projects already facing high development and construction expenses. Mortgage rates depend more directly on longer-term bond yields and mortgage market conditions. The 10-year Treasury yield stood at approximately 5%, down from more than 5.3% earlier this month. That decline provided some relief for housing demand, although long-term borrowing costs remain elevated. Demand for capital associated with data center and AI investment, concerns over federal budget constraints, and oil supply risks and diesel price pressures related to the Iran war remain important considerations for the rate outlook. Overall, the October meeting combines a stronger assessment of economic growth with a decision to wait on additional inflation data. Possible productivity gains provide a potential path toward continued expansion with lower inflation, but the Fed is seeking more evidence that price stability is on the horizon. For housing, the key question remains whether price pressures can ease without another increase in borrowing costs. Chairman Warsh also announced that in 2027, the Fed will hold seven policy-setting meetings and one strategy meeting. In 2028, there will be six policy meetings and two strategy sessions. items.title: Fed Holds Rates Steady, But Sets Up a December Hike
items.description: Fed Holds Rates Steady, But Sets Up a December Hike Published on October 28th, 2026 by Chen Zhao Takeaway: The Fed skipped hiking rates at today’s meeting, as expected. But they set up a hike at the December 9th meeting. The Fed’s main message: Future hikes may be necessary because the economy is strong and inflation is too high. But they’re also patient, willing to skip hiking at some meetings in the interest of waiting for more data. The committee voted 10-2 to hold rates steady today, as expected. The dissents came from Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Fed Governor Lisa Cook. The dissent from Cook was a surprise because she is generally seen as a dove, and most observers expected the second dissent to come from Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan instead. Chairman Kevin Warsh was clear, however, that they are not done hiking, saying “I’m unwilling and unable to call overall financial conditions tight,” and “We haven’t achieved price stability, but we’re working on it.” An every-other-meeting hike cadence is in line with recent comments from other Fed officials who have also expressed a desire to keep hiking in the face of a stronger economy, but also a willingness to wait for data. Ultimately, the December hike will come down to the data releases between now and then. If the data comes in as expected, a hike feels all but guaranteed. Chairman Warsh also announced a big change for Fed meetings starting next year, setting aside one meeting for big picture deliberation. He was light on details, but starting in fall 2027, the Fed will continue to have eight meetings a year. However, only seven of those will be “live” meetings where the committee will vote on rate policy and release a post-meeting statement. The remaining meeting will be used to discuss broad monetary policy strategy. And in 2028, the ratio will change further with two out of eight meetings reserved for big picture discussion. While a significant change to Fed practice, this announcement is also not so surprising given the Chairman’s desire to fundamentally question how the Fed works. That being said, should economic conditions warrant it, the Fed could always call emergency meetings to adjust rates. Chen Zhao Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics. items.title: Why a spike in price cuts doesn't always signal a housing market shift
items.description: A seller wants to know whether to reduce their asking price. A buyer wants to know how much negotiating room they have. A loan officer wants to help a borrower understand what to expect in the local market. All three need more than the latest inventory count or price-reduction percentage. A market where sellers have been reducing prices for months presents a different set of considerations than one where price reductions have only recently become more widespread. Yet a snapshot of today's data might make those markets look remarkably similar. That's what we're seeing in Brentwood and Oakley, two neighboring California cities where similar housing conditions are masking very different price-reduction trends. For housing professionals, understanding how those conditions developed can be just as valuable as knowing where they stand today. Two markets, two different pricing stories Brentwood and Oakley sit in eastern Contra Costa County, with similar suburban housing characteristics and median asking prices of $775,000 and $717,000, respectively, as of Oct. 23. Over the preceding 12 weeks, both cities recorded approximately nine new pending sales for every 10 new listings. But their price-reduction histories look very different. In Brentwood, an average of 46.5% of active listings had experienced a price reduction during the period, up 6.1 percentage points from the comparable period last year. In Oakley, the average was 37.9%, down 1.6 percentage points year over year. Then the latest readings changed the picture. Oakley's price-cut share climbed from 36.3% on Oct. 2 to 55.4% on Oct. 23, surpassing Brentwood's 48.5%. A comparison of the latest week would show price reductions were more widespread in Oakley. The longer view shows Brentwood has experienced elevated price-cut activity for months, while Oakley's increase is more recent. That difference matters in a listing conversation. In Brentwood, an agent can point to sustained price-cut activity when discussing the competitive environment with a seller. In Oakley, the more relevant observation may be that reductions have become more widespread recently, although it's too early to know whether that change will persist. Neither finding determines the right asking price for an individual property. Both provide useful context for evaluating comparable listings and setting expectations. Why fewer homes for sale doesn't always mean less competition Oakley's recent increase in price reductions isn't the only change worth watching. Between Oct. 2 and Oct. 23, the city's median days on market climbed from 49 to 70. In neighboring Brentwood, the median moved from approximately 46 to 49 days. The simultaneous increase in Oakley's price-cut share and median days on market provides additional context for the recent shift. More active listings have experienced price reductions, and the typical active listing has been on the market longer. Yet Oakley had just 1.6 months of inventory on Oct. 23, compared with 2.4 months in Brentwood. That creates an important distinction for housing professionals. A market can have relatively limited inventory while still showing signs that some listings are facing greater difficulty attracting buyers. For an agent preparing a listing presentation, these trends can help explain why a competitive asking price matters even when available supply appears limited. For buyers, they can provide a reason to examine how long individual properties have been listed rather than assuming that lower inventory means less negotiating opportunity. These measures don't establish what will happen next. But when multiple indicators begin changing together, they give professionals a stronger reason to investigate whether local market conditions are shifting. The county average can hide important differences The broader Contra Costa County data reinforces the point. Over the 12 weeks ending Oct. 23, the county recorded fewer than 100 new pending sales for every 100 new listings, down from approximately 109 during the comparable period in 2025. But neighboring cities experienced that shift differently. In Antioch, the ratio of new pendings to new listings fell from 1.17 to 0.89, a much larger decline than the countywide change. In Pittsburg, new pending sales still outnumbered new listings during the 12-week period. Yet its average price-cut share increased 7.2 percentage points year over year, the largest increase among the five eastern Contra Costa cities examined. The relationship between buyer activity and seller pricing behavior isn't always straightforward. That distinction becomes especially important when a client arrives with a countywide statistic and assumes it describes the conditions in their neighborhood. An agent who can explain where a city differs from the county, and whether that difference is growing or narrowing, can offer more meaningful market context than a county average alone. The central bank’s benchmark rate influences a wide range of consumer borrowing and savings costs. As long as the Fed keeps rates elevated, consumers are unlikely to see much relief from the high prices and higher borrowing costs that continue to weigh on household budgets. watch now VIDEO 5:49 05:49 Barclays' Giannoni sees Fed hiking in Dec and Jan as inflation pressures persist Squawk Box Asia The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, even as rising energy costs threaten to keep inflation elevated and further strain already-tight household budgets. Higher energy prices stemming from the Iran war may prove stickier than expected, but the central bank's decision to hold rates steady gives policymakers more time to assess the economic fallout. The dynamic could also lead Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee to consider raising rates at their December meeting in order to bring inflation down to the Fed's 2% target. For now, however, persistent inflation and higher borrowing costs are compounding affordability challenges for many households, economists say. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, said in a post on Oct. 12 that the war has cost the average American household about $2,000 so far, mostly due to higher energy costs, in addition to heightened interest rate costs. "High-net-worth consumers are enjoying the runup in AI stocks and the value of their equity holdings, and are spending with some gusto," Zandi told CNBC. "Lower- and middle-income consumers are increasingly struggling with falling real wages and high rates, and are much more cautious and careful spenders." How the Fed impacts your money The Federal Reserve's decision to keep rates at the current target range of 3.75% to 4%, and the expectation that more rate increases are in the pipeline, means consumers are unlikely to see much relief from high borrowing costs anytime soon. The Fed influences the federal funds rate, an interest rate benchmark that sets what banks charge each other for overnight lending. That rate ripples throughout the economy, influencing both consumer borrowing costs and returns on savings. Short-term consumer lending rates, such as credit cards, closely track the prime rate, which typically moves in tandem with the Fed's benchmark and is generally about 3 percentage points higher. Longer-term rates, like those on 30-year mortgages, meanwhile, are driven more by inflation expectations and the economic outlook. But even as the Fed's benchmark rate has largely held steady — except for September's 25-basis-point increase — the average credit card interest rate has been trending higher amid concerns of rising delinquencies in the face of stubborn inflation, according to LendingTree. items.title: Despite pausing rate hikes, ‘inflation is too high’: Fed chair
items.description: An article from Despite pausing rate hikes, ‘inflation is too high’: Fed chair The news didn’t surprise apartment investors, who tuned in for signals indicating future rate increases. Published Oct. 28, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images As expected, the Federal Open Market Committee held interest rates steady on Wednesday, following its two-day October meeting. Despite two dissenters who voted to raise the federal funds rate target range by 0.25 percentage points, the FOMC kept it at 3.75% to 4%. For the apartment industry, the news was welcome after the FOMC hiked the federal funds rate target range by 25 basis points in September. “Expectations are clearly for the Fed to stand pat, which helps,” Jeff Brown, CEO and co-founder at T2 Capital Management, told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments ahead of the Fed’s announcement. In a press conference following today's announcement, Kevin Warsh, chair of the Federal Reserve, said the goal was to deliver price stability. He also announced a change to the Fed’s 2028 schedule. It will still meet eight times, but only six will set policy. “As we widen the frame to survey the broad economic and financial picture, real activity is clearly pointing in the right direction,” Warsh said. “That's good news. But inflation is too high.” Multiple multifamily owners and investors said they would watch the announcement closely, even if they don’t expect relief anytime soon. Instead, they wanted to understand what could be coming late in the year and in 2027. Trickle-down effect After multiple rate cuts in 2025 , the Fed held rates steady before raising them in September, a move that affected the multifamily market. While “cap rates have moved out since the September meeting,” sellers are slow to accept it, said Tyler Chesser, the co-founder and managing partner of CF Capital. “Historically it takes a few quarters for seller expectations to catch up to the market,” Chesser said. “Until they do, the bid-ask gap means a lot of deals stall, get retraded, or die. I’d expect volume to stay thin through year-end, especially if the Fed signals a December hike.” Smita Garg, principal of investments and asset management at apartment owner and manager SKG Capital, said her firm was closely watching the Fed’s announcement because it “was actively evaluating and executing transactions where today’s cost of capital has a direct impact on pricing and returns.” “Higher borrowing costs continue to make multifamily transactions more difficult to execute,” Garg told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. “Financing costs directly affect what buyers can pay while still achieving appropriate returns, and sellers have not always adjusted expectations to the same degree. That disconnect continues to limit transaction volume.” Forward outlook In its statement, the Federal Reserve said economic activity is expanding at a strong pace, and domestic spending has been resilient, despite geopolitical uncertainty. “Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust,” Warsh said. “Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.” Financial and credit conditions have tightened for some businesses and households after September’s rate hike, according to Warsh. “Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations, and while overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight,” Warsh said. “But broadly, these developments go in the direction of achieving a longer, more durable period of economic growth and price stability.” Still, Warsh said multiple times that inflation remains elevated. “Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy, and that inflation expectations remain as they are anchored,” he said. Warsh said more information is needed before the Fed decides to raise rates again, noting that indicators like oil futures were continuing to rise. “Ensuring price stability … quashing inflation, is not about some fixed individual date on a calendar,” Warsh said. “[The] same way, it's not about some isolated data point.” Tone matters For apartment observers, Warsh’s comments seemed to matter more than the Fed’s decision. Chesser wasn’t surprised by the rate pause, but he wanted to know what comes later. “After September’s hike, the market is trying to read whether another one comes in December, and Chair Warsh’s tone will move the 10-year Treasury more than the decision itself,” Chesser said. “That matters for us because most apartment debt is priced off Treasuries, not the Fed funds rate.” Like Chesser, Garg was also watching Wednesday’s announcement to decipher the Fed’s roadmap into 2027. “For us, the more important question is not necessarily this week’s decision, but the direction of rates over the next six to 12 months,” Garg said. “Greater visibility around the rate path would help bring more certainty back to underwriting and ultimately help buyers and sellers close the gap on pricing.” Regardless, some firms are preparing for higher rates to stick around. “I don't know that we're going to see material drops in rates over the near term,” Greg Cavanaugh, senior vice president of development for the mid-Atlantic region at Bainbridge, told Multifamily Dive. Even with Wednesday’s announcement and Warsh's comments, Chris Nebenzahl, CBRE's Americas head of multifamily research, said the market might not have a clear picture for a few more months. "Greater clarity around the rate outlook should materialize in early 2027, helping bring buyers and sellers back together, improving price discovery and supporting higher transaction volume as investors gain confidence in the market,” he said in emailed comments. items.title: For Fed, politics impossible to avoid in pre-midterm FOMC
items.description: Monetary policy For Fed, politics impossible to avoid in pre-midterm FOMC By Kyle Campbell CloseText About Kyle twitter ByKyleCampbell Published October 28, 2026, 6:00 a.m. EDT | Updated October 28, 2026, 3:23 p.m. EDT 7 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman. Federal Reserve Board Processing Content Key insight: The midterm elections are likely shaping market expectations about the Federal Open Market Committee's policy more than the decision itself. But the political implications are still consequential. Expert quote: "The Fed stresses very much its own independence and its political independence. They wouldn't want to be seen, for instance, raising rates and hurting the administration, the economy in general." — Dan North, senior economist for Allianz Trade Americas The Federal Open Market Committee is broadly expected to keep interest rates unchanged despite signs that inflation is worsening. More than 90% of federal funds futures contracts are pricing in no change to the benchmark rate after Wednesday's meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool, despite nearly 84% of the market anticipating at least one 25 basis point increase before the end of the year. There are several dynamics driving this sentiment. Some economists question the effectiveness of the Fed's policy tools in the current environment. Others are simply following the latest guidance from FOMC participants — outdated as it might be. Then there's the politics of it all. Because of next week's midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years, some analysts believe the Fed will be reluctant to deliver a surprise hike, lest it be seen as putting its thumb on the scale of public sentiment. "We've got the midterms coming up next week, so that is a little bit of a delicate situation," said Dan North, senior economist for Allianz Trade Americas. "I think the Fed will take the position of doing nothing, because if they were to raise rates, that would raise questions about political favor, somehow, on the Federal Reserve. They want to avoid that." President Donald Trump — who stands to lose his governing majority and face myriad congressional investigations into his administration should Democrats take one or both of the houses — is always ready to criticize the central bank for what he sees as partisan policy actions. But North said the issue is not Trump-specific. He would expect the Fed to steer clear of the political fray under any administration. Not because a single rate hike would change the economic outlook dramatically in one week — such changes take months to take effect — but because of the optics. "The Fed stresses very much its own independence and its political independence," North said. "They wouldn't want to be seen, for instance, raising rates and hurting the administration, the economy in general." The historical record on FOMC activity ahead of midterm elections is thin and the results are mixed. Since 1954, the committee has convened in October or early November ahead of a midterm election 11 times, according to data on committee votes maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Those meetings have resulted in three rate hikes, four rate decreases and four instances of no change. For all federal elections — including presidential cycles as well as midterms — the results are similar: the FOMC dropped rates 10 times, raised them six and held them steady nine. There were also 10 election cycles in which the Fed did not vote immediately before ballots were cast but instead, met in late September and again shortly after the election. More recently, rate increases directly before federal elections have become increasingly rare. The committee has approved just one pre-election hike since 1980: a 75 basis point increase directly before the last set of midterms in 2022. That jumbo rate hike was the fourth consecutive three-quarter-point increase by the FOMC, its sixth raise in as many meetings and part of an overall policy tightening campaign that saw the federal funds rate increase more than 5 percentage points in a single year. This is emblematic of other pre-election rate increases. Such moves have tended to be part of hiking cycles that span several consecutive meetings. Read more: As fintechs nab bank charters, what's happening to BaaS? Overheated data center knocked 23 credit unions offline Chris Britt still says banking is broken, but Chime can fix it Credit unions bulk up a business that banks long dominated In theory, the Fed could be at the beginning of such a cycle. The FOMC raised rates in September, most committee members expected to raise at least once more this year and the Fed's primary concern at the moment — persistently high inflation — appears to be trending in the wrong direction . The consumer price index was up 3.7% year over year in September, with input prices rising even more sharply . "All in all, economic data suggest that there is no good reason for the Fed to delay tightening monetary policy," said Jerry Tempelman, former senior analyst at the New York Fed and current vice president of economic and fixed income research at Mutual of America Capital Management. But recent commentary from Fed officials suggests the current tightening campaign might move in fits and starts. In a speech earlier this month, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said he supported the hike last month as a way of shoring up the Fed's credibility, rather than an outright effort to crush inflation. "This was an important step to ensure longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored and to validate the public's confidence that we will achieve our 2% inflation objective in a timely manner," Jefferson said. There is some evidence that market confidence has been restored. Yields for 10- and 30-year Treasuries have declined about 30 basis points

items.title: JLL's Q3 Revenue Surges Amid Strong Leasing
items.description: Strong performance from JLL ’s leasing and capital markets businesses helped the company record strong revenue growth in the third quarter and beat analyst estimates, it announced Wednesday. The brokerage blew past analysts’ consensus earnings estimates, and its stock surged following the Q3 earnings results, up about 12% as of Wednesday afternoon . Google Maps JLL's Houston office JLL CEO Christian Ulbrich downplayed the impact of elevated interest rates on the company’s capital markets business during its third-quarter earnings call, pointing to a strong deal pipeline and his confidence that deals will close on planned timelines. Ulbrich said rates are just one component of capital cost, and property income and rent growth projections can have a far bigger impact on deals than higher debt financing costs. “While bond yields have risen sharply, the interest rate outlook has been well telegraphed and is working through the market in a measured way,” Ulbrich said on the call with analysts Wednesday morning. “Investors are recalibrating their underwriting to adjust for higher borrowing costs and tighter credit structure.” Adjusted earnings per share was up 50% year-over-year to $6.76, beating the consensus analyst estimate of $6.15. JLL announced it intends to execute a new $500M accelerated share repurchase imminently, bringing full-year repurchases to more than $1B. JLL’s revenue was up 12% in Q3 to $7.3B. Leasing advisory growth was up 27% to $941M, led by U.S. growth in industrial, office and data centers, while capital markets services was up 21% to $736M. “This was a good print, in our view, especially considering the concerns/fears surrounding capital markets (interest rate implications) and leasing (tough comps),” analysts from JPMorgan Chase wrote in a note. “On both fronts, we think JLL provided some comfort with a generally positive tone on where the business stands and its own market share gains and margin expansion.” Ulbrich said very few of the company’s capital markets deals “are actually collapsing,” and not many deals are being renegotiated. He said JLL’s capital markets segment is still a very healthy business, especially in the U.S. “The pipeline in itself is actually still growing,” Ulbrich said. “What is happening is that deal time to close is getting a bit longer. It's more intense price negotiations.” On the leasing front, Chief Financial Officer Kelly Howe said the company is seeing an increase in transaction volume and deal sizes across asset classes. In office, JLL’s U.S. clients in the technology and artificial intelligence industries are looking for large swaths of space, she said. Additionally, growth rates in gateway markets have been significantly higher than in nongateway markets, leading to larger office deal sizes. On the industrial side, some of the brokerage’s clients are looking for larger blocks of high-end warehouse space, contributing to deal growth. Data center leasing can be “a bit lumpy” from quarter to quarter, Howe said, but in Q3, the asset class contributed 5% to total leasing revenue. “We feel good about the underlying drivers of our leasing business,” Howe said. “We think we've got momentum going into the fourth quarter.” JLL’s capital markets revenue was up about 21% through the first three quarters, but the company’s full-year guidance projects revenue in the midteens, with implied fourth-quarter growth flat up to low single digits. Howe and Ulbrich said tough Q4 2025 comps were the driver behind its forecast. The company’s capital markets business brought in $854M during the fourth quarter last year. Ulbrich said the company still has a lot of confidence that most of its capital markets deals planned for Q4 will close then and that not many will fall into 2027. “The question around the increase in interest rates is something which makes it a bit more unpredictable,” Ulbrich said. “Our forecast is probably a bit on the cautious side.” Ultimately, rate predictability is more important for markets than the actual yields, Ulbrich said. If volatility declines and the rate environment becomes more predictable, then capital markets will “immediately” start to increase transaction volumes, he said. “Volatility is worse than the absolute level we are on,” Ulbrich said. “People can live with 5% interest rates. We had many, many years where we had to live with that type of interest levels, and we would have said at the time that's fairly low. Now we have to get used to those types of levels again.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Christian Ulbrich , JLL , JPMorgan Chase , Kelly Howe

items.title: Meet the Dallas 500: Linda Silver, Perot Museum of Nature and Science
items.description: Advertisement Live Poll Live Poll In 2027, Linda Silver will reach her 10-year anniversary as the Eugene McDermott CEO of the Perot Museum of Nature and Science. Her leadership continues to steer the museum forward, with initiatives including an upcoming $155 million expansion set to double the Perot's exhibition space . Beyond her work with the museum, Silver is a bit of a globetrotter, having visited 114 countries. She even spent some time in the United Arab Emirates working for the Abu Dhabi government. Museums, however, are a mainstay in her career; she previously held roles at the Great Lakes Science Center in Cleveland, Ohio, and the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County. Read on for more insight on Silver's leadership strategies, guilty pleasures, and her affinity for the arts. Get to Know the Perot Museum's Linda Silver Education: University of Southern California (EdD), Pepperdine University (MBA), University of California, Los Angeles (BA) Birthplace: Marin County, California Destinations of Choice: “From a practical perspective, I enjoy visiting other science museums throughout the world to learn firsthand how other institutions succeed (or don’t) and how that knowledge might be applied to the Perot Museum. But when I’m not touring museums, I like to visit family and friends in Marin County, California, or add to my growing list of countries visited." Hobby/Passion: “I love to read, but my most surprising hobby/outlet is watching K-dramas. I only watch in Korean, and I think because I love to read, the subtitle format allows me to indulge in two hobbies at once.” Go-To Interview Q: “What would your current boss tell me is your greatest talent and your biggest area for growth?” Industry Change: “Our biggest opportunity arises out of our biggest challenge: economic uncertainty. With the economy in great flux, it can be difficult to attract visitors, but it also gives us the opportunity to share why the Perot Museum experience is so invaluable, especially given the transformative impact that high-quality STEM experiences can have, as well as its ability to inspire young learners to pursue high-paying STEM careers in their future. Science museums play a critical role in the STEM-learning ecosystem, and we need to keep working hard to make that connection for our community.” Must-Read: “I read Lost City of the Monkey God, by Douglas Preston, in two days, and I highly recommend it. I'm intrigued by the new technologies that are being applied to more traditional scientific pursuits (in this case LiDAR and archaeology).” Favorite Concert: “Prince on his Purple Rain tour at the Cow Palace in the San Francisco Bay Area. Visceral talent!” Biggest Risk: “I moved my family to the Middle East at the beginning of the Arab Spring in 2011, having only visited the region once for an interview trip. We ended up staying seven years, made friends from all over the world, and traveled to countries we never would have visited from the U.S. I tell young people that taking time to live outside the U.S. or your country of origin is one of the most important educational experiences you can give yourself.” Key Strategies: “Today’s workforce­­—their interests, their level of engagement, their expectations—is always changing, so having adaptable strategies is key. There’s no one-size-fits-all strategy, but as a leader of a mission-driven nonprofit, it’s critical to make sure everyone in the organization understands how their role, big or small, contributes to our mission to inspire minds through nature and science. Clarity on how one’s role fits into the larger puzzle leads to higher engagement and better results.” Greater Good: “I am a long-time supporter of the arts, and Dallas is such a great city for experiencing art and culture. I’ve been a Texas Ballet Theater season ticket holder since moving to Dallas.” Future Forecast: “Our biggest opportunity arises out of our biggest challenge: economic uncertainty. With the economy in great flux, it can be difficult to attract visitors, but it also gives us the opportunity to share why the Perot Museum experience is invaluable, especially given the transformative impact that high-quality STEM experiences can have, as well as its ability to inspire young learners to pursue high-paying STEM careers in their future. Science museums play a critical role in the STEM-learning ecosystem, and we need to keep working hard to make that connection for our community.” Campaign Slogan: “It’s a common refrain in the nonprofit world, but my slogan would be ‘no margin, no mission.’ A worthwhile mission requires the means to execute and deliver, and that means strong financial stewardship.” Lesson Learned: “That uncertainty might be the new normal. While I thought we were finally stabilizing operations following the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent shift of visitor behavior, recent economic challenges have thrown even more uncertainty in our path. Nimbleness and a willingness to make decisions and changes quickly are much more a part of my day-to-day now.” Guilty Pleasure: “ Buc-ee’s Beaver Nuggets and Diet Pepsi (sadly, no nutritional value!)” Read next Business CEO Linda Silver Is Reimagining the Perot Nature and Science Museum The museum is celebrating its first decade and its CEO aims to deepen its impact through digital offerings, gamification, outdoor programs, and more. items.title: Homeownership Rate Rises to 65.5%
items.description: Homeownership Rate Rises to 65.5% October 28, 2026 Na Zhao No Comments The latest homeownership rate reached 65.5% in the third quarter of 2026, according to the Census’s Housing Vacancy Survey (HVS). While this was a modest quarterly decrease, the broader picture continues to reflect significant affordability challenges. With mortgage interest rates remaining elevated, and housing supply still tight, housing affordability is at a multidecade low. Compared to the peak of 69.2% in 2004, the homeownership rate is currently 3.7 percentage points lower and remains below the 25-year average rate of 66.3%. Compared to the previous year, homeownership rates decreased in three age groups. Householders aged 35-44 experienced the largest drop, declining by 1 percentage point from 61.1% to 60.1%. Among younger households, the homeownership rate for those under 35 increased 0.9 percentage points to 36.6% in the third quarter of 2026. This age group is particularly sensitive to mortgage rates and the inventory of entry-level homes. The 55-64 age group saw a 0.6 percentage point decrease, declining from 76% to 75.4%. Homeownership rates for householders ages 65 years and over inched up by 1.2 percentage points over the same time, followed by 0.4 percentage point increase for 45-54 age group The national rental vacancy rate inched up to 7.6% for the third quarter of 2026, on a steadily increasing trend since 2023. Meanwhile, the homeowner vacancy rate stayed at 1.2%. The upticks in both homeowner and rental vacancy rate signal an increase in the existing home supply . The housing stock-based HVS revealed that the total number of households increased to 134 million in the third quarter of 2026 from 133.2 million a year ago. This increase was driven by both owner and renter household growth. items.title: Home Prices Are Falling Fastest in These Cities, Giving Buyers an Edge
items.description: Home prices are declining rapidly in many of the largest U.S. housing markets , with one Texas metropolitan area seeing asking prices fall nearly 10% in a single year. Austin, TX, had the largest drop in median listing prices in September, followed by Memphis, TN, and Tampa, FL, according to the Realtor.com® September Housing Report . The listing price for homes in the Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos metro area decreased by 9.8% from last year to $446,450. Memphis, TN-MS-AR, was second with an 8.7% decrease, and Tampa-St. Petersburg-Clearwater, FL, was third with a 6.6% decrease. Nationally, the median listing price decreased by 1.4% from last year to $419,250 in September, according to Realtor.com data. This price was down 1.4% from last September, marking an 11th consecutive month of year-over-year declines . Among the 50 largest metro areas, these 10 saw the biggest annual declines in listing prices in September: Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, TX: -9.8% Median listing price: $446,450 Memphis, TN-MS-AR: -8.7% Median listing price: $299,950 Tampa-St. Petersburg-Clearwater, FL: -6.6% Median listing price: $385,398 San Diego-Chula Vista-Carlsbad, CA: -6.3% Median listing price: $888,450 Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim, CA: -5.9% Median listing price: $1,034,500 Denver-Aurora-Centennial, CO: -4.9% Median listing price: $569,900 Phoenix-Mesa-Chandler, AZ: -4.8% Median listing price: $475,000 St. Louis, MO-IL: -4.7% Median listing price: $285,950 Washington-Arlington-Alexandria, DC-VA-MD-WV: -4.6% Median listing price: $572,150 Providence-Warwick, RI-MA: -4.2% Median listing price: $569,450 Austin, which saw the largest annual drop, also had an 8.4% decrease in its median list price per square foot—a measure that controls for the size of homes on the market—compared to the previous year. Total active listings in the Austin area were up 1.4% from a year ago, and new listings were up 2.1%. Loading... Austin, TX (above), had the largest drop in median listing prices in September, followed by Memphis, TN, and Tampa, FL. Raymond/Adobe Stock Memphis, where the median listing price decreased to slightly less than $300,000, saw active listings increase 8.1 % from a year ago. New listings, however, decreased 4.6%. Tampa's median listing price decreased 6.6% to $385,398, while the price per square foot decreased 6.0%. California 's two metro areas in the top 10 continue to be some of the most expensive housing markets in the country. San Diego's median listing price decreased 6.3% to $888,450, while Los Angeles' median listing price decreased 5.9% to just over $1 million. Both metros also reported annual decreases in the price per square foot. Denver and Phoenix, two markets that experienced significant housing demand during the COVID-19 pandemic-era boom, also saw asking prices decrease. Denver's median listing price decreased 4.9% to $569,900, while Phoenix's decreased 4.8% to $475,000. St. Louis saw listing prices decrease 4.7% and active listings increase 16.3%. In Washington, DC, listing prices decreased by 4.6% while active listings increased by 16.2%. Both metro areas now provide buyers with more homes to choose from than they did a year ago. Providence, RI, had the smallest decrease among the 10 metro areas, with its median listing price dipping 4.2% to $569,450. However, its median listing price per square foot increased 8.4% from last year. Price cuts continue to be an indication of pressure on the fall housing market. Nationwide, sellers continue to lower their expectations, according to the Realtor.com September 2026 Monthly Housing Trends Report . In September, 20.8% of all active listings had a price reduction, which was 0.9 percentage points higher than a year ago and the largest share for the month since 2018. Active inventory increased 5.4% year over year to over 1.16 million homes, bringing supply to within 9.1% of normal pre-pandemic levels. At the same time, the number of homes under contract decreased 4.1% from a year ago, marking a second consecutive monthly decrease and the largest annual decrease since March 2025. items.title: Essex ups 2026 guidance amid vigorous Northern California performance
items.description: An article from Essex ups 2026 guidance amid vigorous Northern California performance “West Coast multifamily fundamentals offer a compelling case for continued growth above the U.S. average,” CEO Angela Kleiman said on the REIT’s third-quarter earnings call. Published Oct. 28, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Essex Property Trust’s West Coast portfolio saw property revenues grow in the third quarter, driven primarily by the red-hot Northern California market, the San Mateo, California-based REIT reported in its third-quarter 2026 earnings release . Despite the uncertain outlook for the U.S. economy and labor market, “West Coast multifamily fundamentals offer a compelling case for continued growth above the U.S. average,” CEO Angela Kleiman said on the REIT’s earnings call Wednesday. Deliveries are expected to remain low next year, while “technology center innovation continues to attract investment and drive economic activity, supporting our expectation for job and income growth.” The firm slightly upped its full-year 2026 guidance for net income per diluted share, core FFO per diluted share, same-property revenue and same-property NOI. Essex had also raised its guidance in Q2 . Essex’s net income per diluted share in Q3 stood at $1.52, down 40.6% compared to $2.56 in Q3 2025, due primarily to gains on the sale of real estate and land recognized in Q3 2025. Driven by same-property revenue growth, the company’s core FFO per diluted share increased by 0.8% YOY, exceeding the midpoint of its guidance range by $0.01 per diluted share. The REIT saw strong renewals in the third quarter, with Northern California leading the pack, according to Kleiman. Concessions were similar to Q3 last year, at about 10 days, although Essex is offering almost no discounts at its Northern California properties. Regional matters With Northern California's booming tech sector, Essex saw a blended rent growth of 7.3% in the region in Q3, “elevated by a strong leasing season with an extended peak that continued through September,” Kleiman said. Within NoCal, Santa Clara, San Mateo and San Francisco counties outperformed, while Alameda and Contra Costa lagged. Market rents are still catching up in San Francisco, and Kleiman sees plenty of room for more growth. “Just to return to pre-COVID affordability levels, rents could actually increase by over 20% with no wage growth,” Kleiman said. The rent-to-median income ratio in San Francisco currently sits at 25.7%, compared to the 20-year average of just under 30%, according to Kleiman, while Oakland and San Jose are seeing ratios of around 21%. “Affordability remains a tailwind in this market for us, and we continue to have conviction that there's more room to run there,” Kleiman said. Seattle has gradually recovered from a soft start to the year, led by the east side, where tenants are migrating from downtown and other markets, according to Kleiman. The city’s tech jobs are recovering, “and with the office expansion announcements that occurred last year and as supply deliveries continue to decline, we do anticipate that Seattle will have a nice rebound toward the end of next year,” she said. Southern California’s operating conditions remain stable, with Orange County and San Diego performing most strongly in the region, according to Kleiman. She expects to see a lift there from the defense and aerospace industry, which is estimated to surpass $1.5 trillion in the next decade, with “a third of that funding allocated in Southern California.” BY THE NUMBERS Category Q3 YOY Change Revenue $449.9 million 3% Net operating income $313.2 million 3.1% Operating expenses $136.7 million 2.8% Core FFO $4.00 0.8% Average rent $2,777 2.5% Occupancy rate 96.3% 30 bps SOURCE: Essex With SpaceX’s engineering and manufacturing headquarters in the Los Angeles region and Anduril Industries building a new campus in the Long Beach area, “two major industry giants having a footprint in those markets is a very good indication,” Kleiman said. That said, “these are relatively new, and money is just getting allocated. Companies are just starting to hire, and so it would be way too early to see that translate to job growth.” There are “green shoots in LA,” where housing supply has fallen more than 40% over the past two years, according to Kleiman. Even though there have been more entertainment industry layoffs, they make up a small portion of the economy, while professional services remain stable. Essex’s Q3 activity One drag on results was legal settlements. Essex agreed to resolve its case related to RealPage in July for $36.5 million and spent $19.3 million on another litigation matter, per the earnings report. Essex paid the second sum to settle a class-action lawsuit alleging it wrongly withheld security deposits , the Times of San Diego reported. In September, the firm obtained a $275 million unsecured term loan that matures in three years, with two one-year extension options. In the third quarter, Essex sold three apartment communities for a pro rata contract price of $111.9 million, including a 76-unit community in Seattle for $30 million, according to its release. On Tuesday, the firm also closed on a 474-unit community built in 2022 in the East Bay area of Northern California, Kleiman announced on the call. “Priced over $200 million and well below replacement cost, this asset is expected to generate a mid-5% yield,” Kleiman said. Essex bought another 378-unit apartment community built in 2024 in Oakland, California, after the end of Q3, per its earnings report. West Coast transaction volume for institutional assets in Q3 was comparable to last year, according to Kleiman, but with “ recent increases in the Treasury rates is still being factored into the transaction market, it would not be a surprise if fourth quarter volume declines as buyers and sellers adjust to the new rate environment.” Click

items.title: Open Real Estate gains momentum as independent brokerages sign on
items.description: For Donny Samson, the CEO and principal broker of Virginia-based RealTrends Verified Samson Properties , the decision to have his firm join Open Real Estate as one of the first participating brokerages was a no-brainer. “I have been pretty outspoken over the last year or two about consumers having the ability to see all the options,” Samson said. “In the [D.C.-Maryland-Virginia] market, there are a lot of listings that are not fully visible to the public and that has been a frustrating process for them. I’ve just been so passionate about making every listing available for everybody to see, as it is the best for sellers and buyers, that I think that caught the attention of the founders.” Samson said AGNT CEO and 2026 HousingWire Vanguard award winner Leo Pareja , who he considers a friend in the industry, reached out to discuss Open Real Estate and that before Pareja was done explaining the idea, he was ready to sign on. “I don’t want to be in a world where three years from now sellers are going to have to list with seven agents in order for their listings to get in front of buyers,” Samson said. Getting in at the ground level Launched on Monday by AGNT, (the parent company of eXp Realty and NextHome franchises), HomeServices of America , Keller Williams Realty and Real REMAX Group , all RealTrends Verified brokerages, Open Real Estate is a “national residential real estate data-sharing initiative.” The founders of the initiative have specified that this is not a national MLS nor are they seeking to replace local MLSs, but rather an initiative seeking to “streamline the distribution of property information, expand access to housing inventory and support a more open, competitive housing marketplace.” Samson said he is proud that his firm is one of the first participating brokerages. “I feel honored,” he said. “I feel like we are on the right side of this issue.” While not one of the four initial participating brokerages, RealTrends Verified GameChanger Iron Valley Real Estate announced it had signed on to Open Real Estate just hours after the news broke. “When I saw it come across, I jumped on it right away and spoke with my business partner, and we felt like it was the right thing for us to do,” Rob Cleapor, the CEO of Iron Valley Real Estate, said. “We believe in an open, cooperative marketplace because we feel that it gives the consumer more opportunities. We felt like it was the right thing to do for the industry and for the consumer.” Cleapor added that he hopes Open Real Estate preserves the inter-brokerage cooperation the U.S. housing market is known for as it creates a better transaction experience for consumers and it allows buyers and sellers to work with the agent they want, not the agent with the access to the largest private network. “I don’t think buyers should ever have to sacrifice their ability to choose an agent based on trust, service and expertise,” Cleapor said. “That is what I’m really hoping comes out of this.” Antitrust red flags But in a post-Sitzer/Burnett environment , cooperation among real estate brokerages doesn’t come without some concern regarding antitrust enforcement. For Samson though, this was not a concern. “It sounds silly, but when you hear that the four companies that have been so vocal about this issue are the founding members, and they want everyone to be included, I felt like they wouldn’t be out talking to me about it if they hadn’t run everything through with their lawyers and dotted their ‘Is’ and crossed their ‘Ts.’ I understand that antitrust is a touchy subject, but I can’t imagine how something we are trying to do for the betterment of the consumer experience could be something that could be litigiously come after,” he said. Cleapor added that cooperation among competitors has always been at the center of the U.S. real estate industry. “Our fiduciary duty is always for the consumer,” Cleapor said. “So, I think, as long as everyone that is involved with this — all of the brokers, owners and brokerages — always have the best interests of the consumers at heart, I don’t think we have to worry about antitrust laws.” Open for opportunities Although it is still early days for Open Real Estate, which is expected to launch in Q1 2027 , Samson said he is hopeful that all other brokerages join the initiative. “In my perfect world everybody would be singing from the same sheet of music, and we’d all be reading the same book,” Samson said. “Open Real Estate is a system that was created by agents with the mindset that we know what information we need and that we are putting it in one depository that will make it easier for us to disperse to MLSs, portals and any other site that needs good, clean data, not fragmented data from some brokerages and not others. This is what would be best for buyers and sellers.” Samson said it would be easy for brokerages to stick their head in the sand and pretend that everything is fine, but he believes it is important to be part of an initiative that he feels is working to create a better experience for consumers and agents. “Samson Properties wants to be part of the solution and part of creating a better environment moving forward," Samson said. Cleapor added that while every brokerage needs to make the right choice for their business, culture, values and goals, if they want to preserve a market where buyers can see all available inventory and sellers understand their marketing options, joining Open Real Estate should be something they consider. “The public is seeing a lot of negative in the real estate space right now, from brokerages and MLSs suing each other, to high mortgage rates and a slow market, but I hope with Open Real Estate we can create a positive message for the consumer, so they feel confident in the real estate industry and that agents have their best interest in mind,” Cleapor said. items.title: ANALYSIS: The Fed Holds Steady but the Cost of Capital Does Not
items.description: National CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. National + Finance | October 28, 2026 By: Joe Palmisano ANALYSIS: The Fed Holds Steady but the Cost of Capital Does Not The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady Wednesday, pausing after September’s increase as policymakers weighed persistent inflation against the effects of higher borrowing costs. The decision has shifted attention to the timing of another potential hike and whether elevated Treasury yields will continue tightening financial conditions on their own. The Federal Open Market Committee maintained its target range at 3.75% to 4.00%, as expected. Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, preferring a quarter-percentage-point increase. The decision followed July’s hold, which drew three dissents favoring higher rates from Hammack, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan. Fed Upgrades Economic Assessment The committee acknowledged that inflation remains too high but said additional information would help it “determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee’s 2% goal.” Policymakers also strengthened their assessment of economic activity, describing growth as proceeding at a “strong pace,” compared with a “solid pace” in September. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient,” the committee said. “Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.” The decision leaves policymakers balancing economic resilience against price pressures that have shown signs of accelerating rather than converging toward their target. “Despite noise to the contrary, no change represents the most logical course of action at this juncture,” said Tom Briney, president and chief investment officer at Origin Credit Advisers. Maintaining rates, he said, allows earlier policy changes to work through the economy before officials make another move. December Hike Remains in Focus While the timing remains uncertain, market participants largely viewed Wednesday’s decision as a pause, rather than an end to tightening. “The Fed did what was largely expected today, punting on a likely rate hike until the December meeting,” Eric Winograd, chief U.S. economist at AllianceBernstein, told Connect. Winograd said the committee’s core remains optimistic that inflation will ease, limiting the need for additional increases. Waiting provides more data to test that outlook. Bryan Jordan, chief strategist at Cycle Framework Insights, also expects tightening to resume in December. “There are still too many economic crosscurrents, and uncertainty is still too elevated to allow an overly aggressive policy stance,” Jordan told Connect. “With inflation remaining well above the 2% target, the Fed risks losing credibility if it stays on the sidelines for much longer.” Treasury Yields Tighten Financial Conditions The 10-year Treasury yield has reversed its relentless move higher since September’s meeting. After rising following the start of the Iran war, it peaked at 5.32% earlier this month before retreating to around 5% Wednesday, roughly its level at the previous Fed meeting. “Today’s pause doesn’t mean the Fed is done tightening — it means the Fed is letting the bond market do some of the work,” Erik Aarts, vice president and senior fixed-income strategist at Touchstone Investments, told Connect Money. Aarts said September’s increase and higher long-term rates have already tightened financial conditions. He favors high-quality, intermediate-maturity bonds without relying on a sharp decline in long-term yields. Christian Salomone, chief investment officer at Ballast Rock Private Wealth, said investors will watch the yield curve and whether persistent inflation, fiscal deficits and heavy Treasury issuance push longer-term yields higher. Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, emphasized that borrowing conditions can tighten even when the Fed leaves its benchmark unchanged. “Any lasting market relief would depend on greater confidence that inflation is cooling enough to reduce the need for further hikes,” he told Connect. Real Estate Owners Weigh Financing Alternatives For commercial real estate, Treasury yields remain a more direct financing consideration than the Fed’s overnight policy rate. “The direct determinant of our cost of funds is the five- or ten-year treasury rate,” Michael T. Cohen, principal at Williams Equities, told Connect. He described Fed rate decisions as a “blunt tool” that can eventually influence demand and inflation. Rate volatility is also changing how property owners approach transactions. “Increasingly, we’re seeing owners pursue a third option between accepting today’s pricing and walking away from a deal entirely: bridge financing,” said Scott Singer, principal and co-lead of tri-state debt and equity finance at Avison Young. Such financing can provide immediate liquidity while preserving the ability to sell later, Singer said. Competitive lending for quality properties is also giving borrowers refinancing alternatives. Longer-Term Inflation Confidence Holds Despite near-term inflation concerns, Michael Underhill, chief investment officer at Capital Innovations, said market-based inflation expectations remain broadly consistent with levels seen before the global financial crisis and only modestly above averages in the five years afterward. “In other words, markets continue to signal confidence that the Federal Reserve will ultimately do what is necessary to keep longer-term inflation expectations anchored and price pressures contained,” Underhill told Connect.
