items.title: Fed Holds Rates Amid Treasury Yield Surge
items.description: Officials at the Federal Reserve voted to hold the central bank’s benchmark interest rate flat Wednesday, capping a volatile month after the central bank's meeting in September, when it raised rates for the first time since 2023. Flickr/Federal Reserve Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at a press conference Wednesday. The decision to hold rates was widely expected , but it comes against a backdrop of elevated inflation that remains stubbornly above target and rising U.S. Treasury bond yields that are putting pressure on borrowers and debt markets, stifling transaction activity. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh opened the customary post-decision press conference with an uncharacteristic look behind the central bankers’ thinking, explaining the decision to sit tight. “At each policy meeting, my colleagues and I assess the economy by looking out the window — it's what we call interrogating reality to gauge what's really going on," he said. “It is not a task that has grown easier.” The vote included two dissents, with Lisa Cook, a President Joe Biden appointee, and Beth Hammack, a rotating member of the voting committee from the Cleveland Fed, voting in favor of a 25-basis-point hike. In its post-decision commentary, the central bank said economic activity was expanding at a strong pace, as opposed to the solid pace it cited after the September meeting. During the press conference, Warsh also announced that the Fed would vote on interest rates one fewer time in 2027 than this year while still holding eight meetings. Warsh expects two fewer votes on rates in 2028, while still meeting to discuss monetary policy. Yields on 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds ticked up after the meeting to 5.04%. They surpassed 5.3% on Oct. 5, the highest level since 2002, and were hovering right above 5% on Wednesday morning, a threshold that market watchers have long warned threatens to slow economic growth. They moved modestly upward on the Fed's decision. “Holding rates today doesn’t undo what the last two months have done to commercial real estate deals,” Mitch Ginsberg, founder of mortgage broker CommLoan, said in an email. “We’ve seen lenders come back at final loan approval with a higher rate than the one borrowers planned around. With the midterms next week and a December hike largely priced in, that uncertainty isn’t going away.” The rising cost of debt is leading to more distressed trades , deals being repriced or pulled and heightening refinancing risk of existing commercial mortgages. Roughly 78% of fixed-rate securitized commercial real estate debt maturing through 2028 carries an interest rate below the current 10-year Treasury yield, Newmark estimates. Inflation has for years run ahead of the Fed’s stated 2% target, with President Donald Trump ’s trade war and tariffs first driving up prices before the U.S. began a war with Iran that spiked energy prices and rippled across the broader economy. Warsh recommitted the Fed to bringing inflation down, a point he's frequently repeated at every meeting, but said a single data point would not drive decisions. "Quashing inflation is not about some fixed individual date on a calendar, the same way it's not about some isolated data point," he said. Warsh signaled at the press conference that the first rate hike had already cooled market activity, and framed the issue more around timing. The tone was somewhat doveish, Stephen Buschbom, Trepp’s head of applied research and analytics, told Bisnow. "Warsh stopped just short of saying that the market is doing some of the work for them," he said, adding that he'd be watching to see if odds began to shift towards a more restrained monetary policy path. Inflation nudged slightly higher to 3.7% in the September Consumer Price Index report . Core inflation, which strips out food and energy costs, was up a more modest 2.6%. Traders briefly shifted bets toward a rate hike earlier this month after the CPI report but shifted back toward no rate change after a weak jobs report came later in the month. Nonfarm payrolls were up just 29,000 roles in September, less than half the 84,000 forecast. August and September data was also revised down from what had been strong results, with 60,000 fewer jobs than previously reported. The rate decision comes six days before the midterm elections, which are expected to be heavily influenced by voter dissatisfaction with the economy , particularly rising prices. Democrats are projected to win back the House of Representatives, and the race for the Senate is a toss-up, according to Cook Political Report . Warsh said the upcoming election had no bearing on the central bank's decision, noting that the upcoming month before the December meeting was an "information-rich interval" that would give Fed members good data to act on. Real estate investors, many of whom had hoped to close deals by the end of this year, don't have the same luxury. “The midterm elections add another layer of uncertainty, and until the political picture clears, expect to see many buyers and sellers choosing to sit on the sidelines,” Louis Puopolo, head of the New York City Commercial Division at Douglas Elliman , said in an email. items.title: Post-2022 loans drive 43% of foreclosure starts; act early
items.description: Servicing Post-2022 loans drive 43% of foreclosure starts; act early By Colin McNamara Published October 28, 2026, 5:43 a.m. EDT | Updated October 28, 2026, 4:52 p.m. EDT 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email What's at Stake: Mortgage servicers risk rising defaults if they fail to spot early borrower distress. Supporting Data: 43% of September's foreclosure starts came from loans originated since 2022. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Recently originated loans are driving the current default pipeline , signaling mortgage servicers should be proactive in identifying financial distress. Processing Content Loans originated in 2022 or later accounted for 43% of September's foreclosure starts and 49% of completed sales, according to the September 2026 ICE First Look report. Because new borrowers have accumulated less equity and face higher borrowing costs, servicers should contact borrowers before they become seriously delinquent and find appropriate solutions to prevent foreclosure. "Today's market landscape highlights the value of risk management systems that can seamlessly adapt as the book changes," Andy Walden, head of mortgage and housing market research at ICE, told National Mortgage News. "That means scaling workflows up and down as delinquency volumes shift, spotting borrower stress early, responding quickly and having systems that keep pace with changing loan mix and program requirements with regulatory compliance at the forefront," he added. Loans originated over the last four years accounted for 36% of active mortgages and 40% of loans that were 90 or more days delinquent or in foreclosure, so their share largely reflects market makeup and the distribution of active loans. Lower-credit-score and high-loan-to-value lending accounted for the bulk of struggling loans, with the majority of 2022-2026 vintage defaults coming from borrowers with credit scores below 660 or down payments of 5% or less, Walden said. The report also showed the national delinquency rate increased 12 basis points to 3.66% last month, which was in line with the seasonal norm. The rate remained 34 basis points below September 2019 and less than every other prepandemic September on record. Loans 30 days or more past due rose 5% year over year, while serious delinquencies were up 21% from a year ago. Meanwhile, foreclosure starts decreased 3% on an annual basis last month, completed sales climbed 15% and active foreclosure inventory jumped 37%, its highest level since early 2019, the report found. Prepayment speed also fell to a 19-month low, as single-month mortality declined by four basis points to 0.59%, marking the sixth straight monthly decline from March's 1.06%. Speeds were down 20% annually as mortgage rates, now sitting comfortably above 7% , continue to suppress prepayment activity. "Serious delinquencies and active foreclosures are drawing renewed attention, and they're also where technology makes the most difference," said Bob Hart, president of mortgage technology at ICE, in a press release Tuesday. "Servicers need to reach homeowners early to help keep them in their homes and move quickly from first contact to an executable workout without manual handoffs." items.title: CoStar wants faster Homes.com growth, is shifting sales into the field
items.description: CoStar Group may have recorded its 62nd consecutive quarter of double-digit annual revenue growth in the third quarter of 2026, but CEO and founder Andy Florance wants more. Company-wide, net new bookings came in at $37 million for the quarter, below expectations. “Our renewal rates remained high, but with a growing multibillion-dollar subscription base, we need to continue to grow high ROI sales force headcount,” Florence, the 2026 HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said on his firm’s Q3 2026 earnings call with investors and analysts Tuesday night. “Our sales team met with hundreds of thousands of clients and prospects, but they lack the scale to reach the hundreds of thousands of additional prospects we have.” According to Florance, CoStar currently has roughly 2,000 sales professionals on staff, down roughly 10% compared to a year ago. Looking ahead, Florance said CoStar is focused on making changes to the Homes.com sales team, which originally launched with a large, centralized inside sales team based out of the company’s headquarters in Richmond, Virginia. “We'll continue to build the Richmond team, but we are shifting most of our growth effort to the field sales professionals with prior real estate and sales experience in our top cities,” Florance said. “Field reps who meet with clients face-to-face are, on average, much more productive than inside sales and having visited prospects and clients with our home field sales teams at the agents' open houses and offices.” For the quarter, Homes.com generated $7 million of annualized net new bookings, despite reducing inside sales reps from a peak of 655 a year ago to 267 today. “When we demo Homes membership to an agent, we consistently achieved close rates above 40%,” Florance said. “The objective is more demos and expanding our field sales team is how we get in front of more agents.” This performance comes a little over six months after activist investor campaigns called on CoStar to divest its Homes.com assets. Overall, CoStar’s residential real estate segment generated $460 million in revenue, up from $373 million a year ago. In total, the company generated $952 million in revenue for the quarter, up 14% annually. Additionally, CoStar Group reported $74 million in net income, up $105 million from a year prior. As CoStar looks to continue to maintain its profitability, executives noted that the firm had achieved $150 million in cost efficiencies so far this year, noting the ongoing expense reviews have identified potential additional savings of at least $200 million, which the firm expects to realize over the next 12 to 18 months. Acquisitions performing well CoStar also called out the performance of some of its recent acquisitions during the call, noting that Matterport’ s subscription revenue was up 11%, direct sales bookings was up 14% and new enterprise customers was up 46% year-over-year during the quarter. Executives added that they expect Matterport to be profitable by the end of 2027. In addition to this, executives also highlighted Zonda ’s performance. CoStar closed its $815 million acquisition of Zonda in late August. According to CoStar, Zonda's pro forma third quarter revenue was $42 million, roughly 75% of which was subscription, which grew 4% despite a difficult new homes market. The company also announced its agreement to acquire survey-grade aerial imagery program Vexcel Group for roughly $730 million in cash. CoStar said it expects the deal, which will be funded with cash on hand and CoStar’s existing revolving credit facility, to close during the first quarter of 2027. Vexcel operates a global aerial imagery and geospatial data program that captures more than 60 million images a year across millions of square kilometers. Its coverage spans more than 45 countries, 320 major global metros and 99.6% of the U.S. population. The firm refreshes major U.S. metros as often as three times per year and flies disaster zones within 24 hours of an event for catastrophe assessment and response. “Rapid technology advances in aerial photography and lidar are enabling Vexcel to produce extremely high-resolution images and survey-grade measurements of land, houses, office buildings, industrial properties, retail properties, apartment buildings, construction sites and other infrastructure in the built environment,” Florance said in the announcement. Following closing, Vexcel will continue to operate its data program under the Vexcel brand and serve its existing customers and partners. CEO Erik Jorgensen and the current leadership team are expected to remain in place. For CoStar, which owns Homes.com, Apartments.com , LoopNet and other marketplaces, Vexcel’s imagery and derived data could support richer listing content, more accurate property attributes, improved lead qualification and new data products for lenders, investors and government clients. items.title: Billionaires Fighting California's Wealth Tax Have Put $333 Million Into Political Ad Machine Ahead of Elections
items.description: California's top earners have mobilized and poured more than $300 million into an aggressive public campaign to defeat the controversial Billionaire Tax Act at next week's midterm elections . The measure, which will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot as Proposition 40, would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on the global assets of roughly 200 Californians with a net worth of $1 billion or more who resided in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026. Championed by a coalition of labor unions, the proposed tax is intended to help fund healthcare for low-income households affected by the the Trump administration's Medicaid cuts. But in the process, it has ignited fierce, bipartisan opposition among California's richest 1%. To eliminate what they view as an existential threat to their business interests, dozens of Silicon Valley billionaires banded together this year to launch Building a Better California , a political action committee. The exceptionally well-funded nonprofit's stated goals include defeating Proposition 40 and, at the same time, supporting two countermeasures. State campaign finance filings reviewed by the New York Times show that roughly 80 deep-pocketed donors, led by Google/Alphabet co-founder Sergey Brin , former Google CEO Eric Schmidt , and prominent investor John Doerr , have spent more than $333 million on the PAC. Brin alone provided $102 million during the first six months of the PAC's existence, before turning off the money spigot and encouraging others to open their wallets. Silicon Valley builds a war chest The tech mogul, whose personal net worth is currently estimated at over $240 billion, according to Forbes, has long been a vocal critic of the billionaire tax. Since the proposal was first introduced, Brin has shifted several Alphabet entities and assets from California to Florida and purchased property in two states: a $51 million Miami megamansion on Florida's Allison Island and a $42 million mansion on the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe . Loading... Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt donated $40 million to the campaign to defeat Proposition 40. Craig Barritt/Getty Images for TIME ; Realtor.com Following in Brin's footsteps, Schmidt and Doerr each contributed $40 million to the cause, followed by Patrick Collison , CEO of Stripe, an online payment processing company, who chipped in $33 million. According to the Times reporting, existing donors to the campaign have been recruiting fellow business leaders to join the fight by contributing cash or stock and becoming actively involved in the PAC. Top venture capitalists, as well as tech entrepreneurs from companies such as DoorDash and Robinhood, have reportedly answered the call. Bipartisan backlash Opposition to the tax extends beyond the tech industry. Outgoing Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom , who had tried and failed to keep the proposal off the ballot , has warned that it would lead to an outflow of capital from California, erode the state’s tax base, and stifle innovation with little to show for itself. Loading... California Gov. Gavin Newsom fiercely opposes the proposed billionaire tax and previously tried to defeat it. Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images A large share of the PAC's war chest has funded statewide advertising to urge California voters to reject Proposition 40 and approve the two rival initiatives. Proposition 41 would require audits of new state special taxes, while Proposition 42 would ban new taxes on personal property, including financial portfolios and retirement savings. If both Propositions 40 and 42 pass but the latter captures more votes, it would invalidate the billionaire tax. Beyond traditional TV ads, the campaign has been bombarding voters with anti-Proposition 40 messaging through streaming services, video games such as SimCity, and old-school paper mailers. According to internal documents reviewed by the Times, Building a Better California is committed to delivering a decisive blow to Proposition 40 on Tuesday to "chill wealth-tax efforts nationally." Spending chasm Records reviewed by the Los Angeles Times show that the anti-Proposition 40 camp is outspending its opponents supporting the measure nearly 10 to 1. Proponents of the tax on California's wealthiest residents have raised $34.3 million, primarily from the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which sponsored the ballot measure. However, most of those funds were spent on collecting signatures to qualify the tax proposal for the ballot, leaving the pro-measure camp with just $1.6 million in its coffers as of Oct. 17, according to the L.A. Times. Operating on a shoestring budget, campaigners have been sending voters emails and text messages urging them to embrace Proposition 40 while rejecting Propositions 41 and 42 backed by the Silicon Valley elites. Speaking to the L.A. Times, Suzanne Jimenez , chief of staff of the healthcare union, downplayed the colossal funding gap. "The billionaires think voters are stupid," she told the outlet. "Their spending also makes our case for us. When billionaires can afford to spend millions a day protecting their fortunes, voters can see that billionaires have plenty of money to spare." She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. items.title: CoStar Acquiring Aerial Imaging Firm Vexcel For $730M
items.description: CoStar Group is taking to the skies with its latest acquisition. But after announcing the purchase of an aerial imaging company along with its third-quarter earnings, the commercial real estate tech giant's stock is hitting some turbulence. Pixabay/Hotshoe55 Arlington, Virginia-based CoStar has reached a $730M all-cash deal to buy Vexcel, which uses manned aircraft and proprietary imaging technology to collect tens of millions of high-resolution aerial photographs a year across 45 countries. CoStar for years has used fleets of cars to capture photographs of buildings for its vast property database. It plans to complement that with Vexcel's aerial photography and use artificial intelligence to "recognize and extract information and features from them," CEO Andy Florance said Tuesday on CoStar's earnings call. "It is clearly aligned with our mission of digitizing the world's real estate with an incredible ability to leverage AI to create proprietary real estate data of durable value," Florance added. Vexcel brought in $140M in revenue over the last 12 months, up 30% year-over-year, with a six-person sales team, Florance said. He said CoStar can supercharge that growth by expanding Vexcel's sales workforce with CoStar's own 2,000-person sales team. Erik Jorgensen is expected to continue as CEO of Vexcel, which will keep operating its data program and serve its customers under its own brand, CoStar's press release says. The deal is slated to close early next year. "By joining CoStar Group, we gain the scale, technology, and resources to broaden our reach, accelerate innovation, and deliver even greater value to customers worldwide," Jorgensen said in the release. The deal continues CoStar's decades-long strategy of growing through acquisitions. In August, it closed the previously announced acquisition of housing data provider Zonda for $815M. The company's biggest acquisition in recent years was the $1.6B deal to acquire 3D imaging company Matterport that closed in February 2025 . During a question-and-answer session with analysts, Florance compared the Vexcel acquisition to Matterport for the way it will continue to operate as its own company. "In terms of exclusivity, I think this works a little bit like Matterport," Florance said. "Matterport continues to grow as a standalone product, but because it's a combined entity with CoStar, the team at Matterport does a great job in making sure their products are responsive to the needs of our product areas, whether it be apartments, LoopNet [or] homes." Matterport's subscription revenue grew 11% year-over-year in the third quarter, and CoStar expects it to be profitable by the end of next year, Florance said. CoStar's overall revenue rose 14% year-over-year to $952M, and its net income totaled $74M, according to its earnings statement, released after markets closed Tuesday. The company raised its full-year guidance for revenue and earnings from its second-quarter estimates. But Wall Street reacted negatively to CoStar's earnings report, with the company's share price plunging by more than 13% Wednesday. Its stock is down 65% over the last year. items.title: Toll Brothers underwrites lots for tomorrow's market, not yesterday's
items.description: As margins for error narrow in homebuilding’s land rules of engagement, boundaries between strategy and tactics have begun to blur. As slower sales , weaker demand, moderating sales prices and declining margins continue to look for a stabilizing floor, homebuilding land acquisition decision-makers now typically take a more discriminating, granular and real-time look at each deal to ensure it measures up to indefinitely challenging selling conditions. While many builders contend with land bought in a stronger market that is now becoming a liability, Toll Brothers has spent the last few years raising its underwriting bar and tightening it further. That approach is shaping more than what the builder will pay for land. It is influencing where Toll considers building, how it structures deals and where it finds opportunity as competitors reassess older purchases. Rob Paul, Texas and Arkansas group president, and Dustin Bowersett, VP of land acquisition for Toll’s Central Florida division, elaborated on the company’s land strategy during a session last week at the HousingWire Homebuilder Summit , moderated by longtime Wall Street housing analyst Dan Oppenheim. That strategy follows a clear thread. Stricter underwriting, a focus on the best locations, selectivity when sellers won’t budge on price and an emphasis on trusted relationships with land sellers all show how Toll Brothers tries to stay out ahead of a slowing market rather than react to it. Toll Brothers raises the bar for new land Toll Brothers began reassessing its underwriting criteria for evaluating land a few years ago. At the time, lots traded aggressively on the expectation that homes would sell quickly and at high margins, particularly in many high-growth Sun Belt markets. Paul noted that Toll Brothers' land committee is getting much stricter when evaluating deals. As market conditions tightened, the company course-corrected its approach and began scoring land based on a combination of gross margin and internal rate of return (IRR). “The increase of that threshold and making the underwriting more strict over the course of the last couple of years has put us in a position where, should the market turn, we retain some value,” Paul said. This underwriting criteria also considers recent sales performance, while discounting sales performance experienced during the spring, since conditions have worsened since then. “The sales in the last…60 to 90 days absolutely drive decisions. We’re starting to look at what’s happened in the last couple of weeks,” Paul said. Essentially, Toll Brothers expects its newer land purchases to pencil even if the market worsens, because they were completed under higher hurdle-rate standards. The finer point is that the market has changed enough to demand a shift in mindset, with Paul arguing that builders should underwrite the conditions they are likely to face, not the ones they operated through earlier in the year. The Toll Brothers “main and main” advantage Since its inception, Toll Brothers has abided by a “Main-and-Main” philosophy, characterized by purchasing lots in the best locations, i.e. Main Street. This strategy makes sense for Toll Brothers, which has the highest average sales price of any public homebuilder in the country, coming in at roughly $1 million nationally. Bowersett noted that, while Toll Brothers’ Central Florida division sells homes between about $350,000 and $5 million, the vast majority of the division’s volume falls in the $850,000 to $1.3 million range. The bulk of those transactions are domestic move-up buyers, but many are wealthy foreign buyers from Latin America. Regardless of where they come from, they seek top-tier locations in neighborhoods with good schools and a high quality of life. Another reason validates Toll Brothers' focus on Main-and-Main locations. Many fringe areas are now struggling as demand for more affordably priced homes softens or stalls. When buyers are plentiful and demand is high, outlying locations can look like smart bets. However, when that demand thins, the gap between prime and peripheral land can widen quickly. Bowersett pointed to Polk County, Florida, a growing suburban and exurban county located between Orlando and Tampa as an example. During the post-COVID building boom, builders aggressively pursued peripheral land in Polk County. Production builders posted strong absorption rates, developers offered relatively attractive lot pricing and deal structures were easier to negotiate. Now, as population growth and demand in Polk County moderate, that submarket has lost some luster. In hindsight, Toll Brothers’s decision not to pull the trigger on opportunities there proved to be prudent. “We decided not to. We stayed in our core markets, and if you look right now…the lots are essentially worthless in some instances,” Bowersett noted. Peripheral markets nationwide mirror Polk County's dynamics. “The fringe is what gets hurt first, period,” Paul said. “When there are fewer buyers, the market gets a little tough. There’s a flight to quality.” Paul said buyer psychology helps explain the phenomenon. Even when homes are comparable on paper, buyers weigh the risk of being wrong about where they buy. “Buyers don’t want to feel stupid. They don’t want to feel dumb. They don’t want to feel like they’re making a mistake,” he said. “There’s safety in a community that’s already half-built-out. There’s safety in a community that has 10 home sites left.” That preference gives established communities an edge over new fringe developments, reinforcing how Toll Brothers thinks about land. A softer market isn’t lowering demand equally across the board. Instead, demand often remains strongest in central, established locations, leaving builders with outer-ring exposure with a weaker hand to play. Land sellers concede on terms before they cut price Despite a more challenging sales environment, Paul said land sellers are mostly standing pat on lot prices. Toll Brothers

items.title: Hof Wonen Acquires 251 Social Homes In The Hague
items.description: Housing corporation Hof Wonen has acquired 251 to-be-built social rental homes in Soza, a new large-scale, mixed-use urban project being developed by Vorm in The Hague. The deal, which follows Achmea Real Estate forward-purchasing 517 rental homes in the project on behalf of PME Pension, unlocks the start of the project’s first phase, the residential complex. The project will create a new urban commercial and residential neighborhood in the Central Innovation District. Hof Wonen/Vivid A rendering of the Soza skyline and canal in The Hague Located at the site of the former Ministry of Social Affairs office complex, opposite the Laan Van NOI train station in the Bezuidenhout district, Soza will offer a total of 1,194 houses for rent and for sale, as well as an office tower, commercial units and green spaces. Following the finalization of the zoning plan and environmental permit in June, the development has advanced significantly toward implementation, with initial residential completions targeted for 2030. Financial terms concerning the Hof Wonen transaction were not disclosed. Thirty percent of Soza's housing will be designated as social housing, and a minimum of 20% will be classified as midrange market, in response to The Hague’s pressing need for affordable housing. The remaining residential space will fall under the private sector segment. The rental units within the residential tower include studio, two- and three-room apartments ranging from 30 square meters to 90 square meters. Next to the residential units, Soza will offer commercial units suitable for a number of tenants, including supermarkets, bicycle repair stores, healthcare services, fitness facilities and hospitality. Approximately 24,000 square meters of multitenant floor space will be available to let in the office building, with lots ranging from 1,100 square meters on the ground floor to a minimum of 700 square meters on the seventh floor. Constructed from timber, the office building is aiming for a BREEAM -NL Excellent certification and will house a rooftop park, cafe, restaurant and other amenities. The Haaglanden region in the Netherlands continues to grapple with a housing shortage, equal to 6.7% of its existing stock and above the national average of 4.8%, according to research from ABF. An additional 25,000 homes would have to be created to reach the 2% policy target, according to housing and rental property platform Pararius. The gap in the rental housing market in The Hague is especially noticeable in the social sector, as there are approximately 90,000 active house hunters and only 8,000 social rental homes available, according to the collaborative housing association Sociale Verhuurders Haaglanden. As a result, fewer people are able to secure a social rental home, with the success rate falling from 13% in 2023 to 10.4% in 2024, and to just 5.8% for applicants responding to advertised homes, according to ABF. The ARM share of applications increased to 11.3% last week, the highest level in more than a year. In an aerial view, two-story single family homes line the streets of a neighborhood on Sept. 23, 2026 in Thousand Oaks, California. Kevin Carter | Getty Images Mortgage rates fell for the second straight week, and that finally brought consumers back to their brokers. A growing share, however, applied for riskier loans at even lower rates. Total mortgage application volume rose 3.4% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, decreased to 7.37% from 7.41%, with points increasing to 0.76 from 0.75, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. "The decline in rates gave borrowers some relief, with applications rebounding slightly, particularly conventional applications," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA, in a release. "Mortgage rates are still more than a percentage point higher than the same week last year and most homeowners still have rates much lower than prevailing market rates." And that is why refinance is still running well behind where it was last year. Applications to refinance a home loan climbed 3% for the week but were 61% lower than the same week one year ago. About half of all borrowers today have a mortgage rate below 4%, according to data from the Federal Housing Finance Agency's National Mortgage Database. Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home rose 4% for the week but were still 18% lower than the same week one year ago. While mortgage rates have pulled back some in the last few weeks, they are still much higher than they were just a few months ago, and home prices are still rising. Potential homebuyers are also worried about the broader economy, and, anecdotally, some agents say buyers are waiting to see the results of the midterm elections. ARMs are considered riskier because they adjust to whatever the current market rate is at the end of their fixed term. items.title: From 59 zoning codes to 1: That’s the goal of this Ohio county’s streamlining plan
items.description: An article from From 59 zoning codes to 1: That’s the goal of this Ohio county’s streamlining plan The Cuyahoga County, Ohio, Planning Commission says its proposal would modernize zoning standards, unlock development and reduce barriers across the county’s jurisdictions. Published Oct. 28, 2026 Ryan Kushner Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google South Euclid, Ohio, is among the first six cities to partner with the Cuyahoga County Planning Commission on a unified zoning code initiative. Retrieved from City of South Euclid on October 28, 2026 First published on Listen to the article 3 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . To address the housing affordability crisis, many local governments are attempting to untangle decades-old zoning codes that can hamper development. The Cuyahoga County, Ohio, Planning Commission this summer proposed not only updating its zoning code, but developing one code to rule them all: a unified zoning code for all 59 of its jurisdictions. The plan, known as the unified zoning code initiative, “provides local governments with modern regulations that streamline development processes while developing a coordinated approach with partnering communities,” Mary Cierebiej, executive director of the Cuyahoga County Planning Commission, said in a news release unveiling the initiative in June. The Planning Commission on Sept. 28 issued a request for proposals to find a consultant to begin developing the code. The initiative has six initial participant cities, including Brook Park, East Cleveland, Euclid, Maple Heights, North Olmsted and South Euclid. Cuyahoga County has 1.2 million residents in cities, villages and townships that range from dense urban areas to small suburban communities, many of which have outdated zoning codes that are often incompatible with deve l opment needs , the commission said. Cleveland, which serves as the county seat, has been in the process of updating and implementing its own form-based zoning code . “Many communities lack updated zoning maps or rely on outdated hard copy versions, further complicating redevelopment efforts,” the Planning Commission said. Localities that opt in to the county’s unified zoning code will be able to adopt, administer and enforce the new code and be part of a centralized online zoning map. “Developing a Unified Zoning Code all communities in the County could use would greatly benefit our community in ensuring we have the most up-to-date zoning code possible,” South Euclid, Ohio, Mayor and Cuyahoga County Planning Commission Board member Georgine Welo said in a news release. Money could be a barrier for some local governments. Comprehensive zoning updates in Cuyahoga County regularly exceed $200,000 per community, according to the Planning Commission. “Many communities seek assistance for full zoning code updates or only have the resources to undertake small pieces at a time,” the Planning Commission said. “The UZC process allows multiple community zoning codes to be updated at once and adds the benefit of regional collaboration and ongoing maintenance support.” The Planning Commission said it anticipates working with a zoning consulting firm, legal advisors and its approximately 20-person in-house staff to maintain the unified zoning code. The initiative has three funding partners: the Cleveland Foundation, Cuyahoga Land Bank and Akron Cleveland Association of Realtors. “Our county is mainly built out, and new approaches are needed to repopulate our communities and build upon existing infrastructure,” Cierebiej said. “The Unified Zoning Code initiative supports neighborhood reinvestment by giving communities a faster, more cost‑effective path to updated zoning.” Recommended Reading For affordable housing fund, Cleveland embraces private partnerships Smart Cities Dive After major zoning reform, Cambridge, Massachusetts, launches dashboard to track housing Smart Cities Dive These 3 housing programs are showing results. items.title: Smittox Brewing Debuts in Oak Cliff With Classic Beers and Hip-Hop Beats
items.description: Advertisement Live Poll Live Poll They say it’s a hard economy for beer right now. Don’t tell the brewers. They’re doing better work than ever. A little while back, I sat drinking a pint and eavesdropping on a table of brewery employees, gathered together from a variety of Dallas-area spots on their day off. They started to compliment each other. One said they’d just started working at a particular brewery, and the others responded that they could tell: its quality had just jumped up. This convivial hangout was on the patio of Dallas’ newest taproom, Smittox Brewing, a block from the Dallas Zoo and across the street from new community space East Dock . Smittox deserves the welcome party. Its gestation was painfully long and its product is very good. As the region’s only Black-owned brewery , Smittox also has an aesthetic unlike its competitors’, with a terrific soundtrack of classic hip-hop and a mural paying tribute to owner Kuumba Smith’s favorite musicians. It’s a comfortable space. The taproom is on the smaller side, well-equipped with board games and a good stereo. A covered patio faces west. It’s good at catching the breeze and watching the sunset. Another core Smittox strength: good beer names. Its IPA is called Rambo Knife, its pale ale Aging Backpacker, and a hoppy red ale goes by My Grandmomma Gave Me That Chain. “I’ve been here since 2022,” Smith tells me one afternoon as we both sip on beers, mine an Outta Order Porter, his a version of the same with added coffee and dulce de leche. “That’s how long it took [to open].” When he first signed the lease, the property looked like an unlikely brewery site: a trio of small white buildings behind a fence, enveloped by wraparound parking. Smith and his landlord faced challenges. The property had once been a mechanic’s shop, then storage space for the Dallas Zoo to put its seasonal decorations. Until Smith tried to get permits, nobody noticed that the previous property owner had combined three lots, fenced them in as one, and built right on the lot lines. Today’s taproom alone sits atop two lot lines. Before Smith could even get started, he and his landlord had to work with Dallas planners to replat the property. That took two years. The brewer spent that time building his brand with collaboration beers at spots like Vector and Oak Cliff . He says now that they remain friends and are on a group chat with other brewers, including at White Rock and Odd Muse, to compare problems and share solutions. “The good thing about the beer community is, a lot of people give you a recipe and they’re like, ‘Go brew it,’” Smith explains. “There’s no secrets. They all come out different. Everybody’s got different water, different systems, [so if] we have the same recipe, the beer’ll still come out a little different.” This is, of course, the same beer community that came out in numbers when Smittox made its debut. Smittox pours its beers inside a former mechanic shop and Dallas Zoo storage facility. Brian Reinhart The property may be replatted and the doors open, but Smith still faces the challenge of building his core audience. This part of Oak Cliff is still a neighborhood in transition; Smith says many current residents are of an older generation, while developers are planning apartment complexes nearby that may still be years from opening. Restaurant Reviews The Indie Oak Cliff Restaurants, Bakeries, and Bars Getting a Fresh Start East Dock, a transformed former ice factory in Oak Cliff, has become a new hub for small locally owned businesses. By Brian Reinhart | October 21, 2026 | 9:16 am The city won’t sleep on this area much longer. It’s not just near the zoo and a DART station; it’s also down the street from brand-new Halperin Park. I-35 was built in 1959 to separate this historically Black neighborhood from the rest of Oak Cliff, and the highway’s brutal march through the area still deprives it of the prosperity that has come to Bishop Arts. Halperin Park boosters claim that the park will help undo those decades of historical damage. If it succeeds, Black-operated businesses like Smittox and neighboring restaurant Barro y Fuego might be proof. For now, though, people focused on the park’s opening should walk down Ewing Avenue. “This whole area needs to get some press,” Smith says. “Everybody’s focusing on the park. Sometimes foot traffic doesn’t come past the corner. If you park at the zoo, you can walk over here.” So far Smittox customers are loving its drinks, vibe, and events, including the unlikely top draw, plant bingo. A taproom mural by tattooist and artist Joe Radnik includes nods to many of Smith's favorite groups: Public Enemy, Souls of Mischief, the Wu-Tang Clan, the Beatnuts, MF Doom, UGK, A Tribe Called Quest, Nervous Records. “The tape could be considered OutKast,” Smith adds. “It’s a part of my culture, experience, and upbringing.” Though Smith is a dark beer drinker by preference , his top seller so far is his fruited blonde ale, Thought Process. “I knew it was gonna do good. I just didn’t know it was going to be our number one seller.” After a stretch when the brewery’s chiller was broken, putting new beers and cans on hold, Smittox is back in full swing. Smith has delivered a few kegs to the zoo for its late-night events. He’s focused now on both continuing to serve a top product and continuing to build this area’s new Oak Cliff community. “We’re trying to figure out how to create a nice system,” he says of Smittox and its neighbors. “A nice neighborhood friendly vibe with East Dock.” I ask if he feels savvy by taking a bet on an up-and-coming neighborhood. “It’s definitely a risk. A lot of sleepless nights. At the end of the day, we just got to play it right.” Smittox Brewing , 930 E. items.description: Advertisement Live Poll Live Poll The Dallas Mavericks announced that CEO Rick Welts is retiring , and Ethan Casson, who was hired as president last year, will become the team’s next CEO and alternate governor. But if you look a little harder, this could be yet another sign that the organization’s plans for a new arena at Valley View are becoming increasingly solid. For one, there is why the two were hired. Welts was hired in part to focus on the team’s next arena. Casson was brought on board, in part, to clear the decks for Welts to do just that. Earlier this year, D CEO spoke to the two , and Welts said Casson’s skill set would help strengthen the team and its position as the organization evolved into “a sports and entertainment company that operates its own arena and district.” With Welts’ retirement, it’s reasonable to infer that one of the biggest questions he was brought in to help answer—where that arena and district would go—is very close to being settled. In July, the team announced that it had hired Legends Global as its owner’s representative. Legends Global said it was hired to act as “an independent third-party representing the Mavericks from pre-design through closeout, protecting the team’s interests in budgeting, construction schedules, quality, and risk control, while also serving as a liaison to contractors and architects.” Last month , the organization said it was ready to begin working with the city to amend a planned development already in existence and create a subdistrict that would allow a sports and entertainment district. Learn More When you ask the Mavericks front office, you’ll invariably hear some hedging—after all, they’ve entered into option agreements to purchase 104 acres of the former Valley View site from three separate owners. That, plus the negotiations with the city, require some delicate responses. But the party line continues to be that the site is Valley View. But more tea leaves emerged this week as Welts sat down with Bloomberg’s Randall Williams during the publication’s Bloomberg Invest Dallas conference. You can watch the full interview here , but the highlights: On coming out of retirement to work with the Mavericks: “Ownership. Market. Opportunity to think about building a new arena again. You know, there’s a reason they call it a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity, because nobody would be stupid enough to do it twice.” (Welts previously helped lead development of Chase Center in San Francisco.) On the scope of the proposed entertainment district and arena in Dallas: “The project that we're envisioning right now is actually much bigger than the project we did in San Francisco with the arena and 10 acres of other development, which was office buildings, retail, restaurants. Here, we have an option to buy over 100 acres in Dallas right now and create an entertainment district much bigger than the one that we did in San Francisco, and an arena. But, you know, it all starts with the arena.” The design process for the new arena: “It's going to set a new level of hospitality, not just for all those people who can afford to have seats on the floor. But there's as much focus on the experience of a fan in the top row of the upper bowl and what that hospitality experience can be—different than what's been done in sports before. So I'm really excited about where we are in the project. We're still five years away. We have a lease at American Airlines Center until 2031. But our goal is that when this audience walks into that building for the first time, their first reaction is, ‘Wow, they get Dallas.’ We don't want to build Chase Center in San Francisco. We don't want to build Intuit Dome in Los Angeles. We want to build something that, when people walk in, they'll feel like we really understand this market and the special nature of North Texas.” Will it really be Valley View? “We have the option to buy 100 acres … in what’s called the Valley View location, which is in Dallas. That’s job number one. We have said from day one that we want to be the team that has Dallas on their jersey that actually has our playing facility in Dallas, and that's what we're planning to do. We're at the beginning of the beginning. It was a seven-year process in San Francisco to get Chase Center built and get the Warriors moved from Oakland to San Francisco. So I wish I could predict what that path was going to look like. But we're very focused right now.” The potential for public money to be involved in the project: “It's a city-by-city decision and what cities feel like they can devote to projects and the value of that project in their city, right? So it's an ongoing discussion we're having with the city right now. It won't surprise you: I'm in the camp that I think these add value to the fabric of a city. items.title: Aging boomers fuel $28 billion investor rush into senior housing
items.description: Housing inventory Aging boomers fuel $28 billion investor rush into senior housing By Shawna Kwan Published October 28, 2026, 9:56 a.m. EDT 1 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Senior housing deals in the US are on pace for a record year as investors rush to capture high returns amid growing demand from the country's aging baby boomers. Processing Content Sales of senior living and care facilities reached roughly $28 billion this year through September, more than any full-year total in data from Newmark Group Inc. going back to 2001. That transaction value is up 111% from the first nine months of 2025, the biggest jump for any real estate class after data centers. The sector has been lucrative for investors, generating 16.2% returns on average in the second quarter, compared with 4.9% for industrial real estate and 4.1% for offices, Newmark said. READ MORE: Boomers, Millennials lead cash-rich buyer opportunities Investors anticipate that an increasing population of elderly Americans will generate a greater need for senior living communities. The oldest baby boomers, born in 1946, are turning 80 this year. The number of Americans who are that age or older is projected to jump more than 50% in the decade through 2035, the US Census Bureau estimates . At the same time, new development has been limited, keeping property values high. "A combination of 80-plus population growth exploding in the US, which is driving the growth and demand for senior housing, and low birth rates in the last 20 to 40 years, which resulted in the dearth of caregivers," is enticing investors to the sector, said Adam Doneger, executive vice chairman of US capital markets at Newmark. READ MORE: Most popular cities for boomers to live High construction costs as a result of inflation, tariffs and elevated interest rates as well as a more complicated development process have constrained the supply of new senior housing, Doneger said. Hines, which has $91 billion of assets under management, is interested in buying senior housing properties in locations that are close to urban centers, said Alfonso Munk, co-head of investment management at the firm. "There is significant demand for senior housing but not enough stock in the US," Munk said. Shawna Kwan Bloomberg News

Earnings Press Release
Invitation Homes Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results
Dallas, TX, October 28, 2026 — Invitation Homes Inc. (NYSE: INVH) (“Invitation Homes,” “we,” “our,” and “us”), the nation’s
premier single-family home leasing and management company, today announced our Third Quarter (“Q3”) 2026 financial and
operating results.


Q3 2026 Highlights
•   Year over year, total revenues increased 6.3% to $731 million, property operating and maintenance costs increased 2.0% to
    $264 million, and net income available to common stockholders increased 15.6% to $158 million, or $0.27 per diluted
    common share.
•   Year over year, Core FFO per share increased 2.4% to $0.48, while AFFO per share increased 0.1% to $0.38.
•   Same Store NOI increased 1.1% year over year on 1.6% Same Store Core Revenues growth and 2.5% Same Store Core
    Operating Expenses growth.
•   Same Store Average Occupancy was 96.4%, a reduction of 10 basis points year over year.
•   Same Store renewal rent growth of 4.3% and Same Store new lease rent growth of (0.2)% resulted in Same Store blended
    rent growth of 3.0%.
•   We sold 658 wholly owned homes, most to families purchasing for their own use, and acquired 216 wholly owned homes,
    for net dispositions of 442 homes and net proceeds of approximately $245 million that we used to fund share repurchases.
•   As previously announced, on July 8, 2026, we closed a public offering of $500 million aggregate principal amount of 4.950%
    senior notes (the “Notes”). The Notes were priced at 99.291% of the principal amount and mature on February 1, 2032. Net
    proceeds were used to prepay a portion of our secured debt obligation maturing in June 2027.


Capital Allocation Update
From December 1, 2025 through October 27, 2026, we bought back nearly $1 billion of our shares. This includes an aggregate
of 36,923,753 shares repurchased to date at an average stock price of $26.78, and represents an implied value per home of
approximately $280,000 against a gross average sales price of approximately $460,000 for homes sold during that same period.


On October 26, 2026, our board of directors authorized an additional $500 million share repurchase program.


Comments from Chief Executive Officer Dallas Tanner
“Our third quarter reflected steady execution across the platform. Same Store NOI grew 1.1% year over year, blended rent growth
was 3.0%, and with the benefit of our share repurchases, Core FFO per share grew 2.4%. Since December 2025, we’ve
repurchased nearly $1 billion of our stock at a substantial valuation discount. We believe that is more than any other residential
REIT. With the new $500 million share repurchase program our board just authorized, we intend to keep funding buybacks with
home sale proceeds whenever our stock trades at a meaningful discount to the value of our homes, guided by market conditions
and a disciplined approach to the balance sheet.”


“Following a solid third quarter, we are raising our full year guidance midpoints for Core FFO per share by $0.01 to $1.96, Same
Store NOI growth guidance to 1.2%, and wholly owned home sales to $950 million, which supports our continued focus on
closing the gap between public and private market values.”

Invitation Homes management that are measures not defined under accounting principles generally accepted in the United States
(“GAAP”). These measures are defined herein and, as applicable, reconciled to the most comparable GAAP measures.
